passage:
Dear Vandana,
You were right when you said I keep circling the thing I want. I want to lead the new regional team. I've wanted it since my first week. But when Mr Sangma asked who would present the budget review to the board, I stared at my notebook until someone else raised a hand.
The truth is, I'm scared that if I try and fumble, everyone will see I'm not as good as they think. Not trying keeps the dream safe. It also keeps it far away.
So I'm trying your idea of small bets. On Friday I'll present just the first slide at our team meeting. Next month, one section at the board review. If my voice shakes, I'll survive it, and then I'll know.
I'll write and tell you how Friday goes.
Lalremsiami

qa.a: Who would present the budget review to the board.

qa.a: Lalremsiami fears fumbling in front of everyone and being seen as less able; not trying keeps the dream safe, even though it keeps it far away.

qa.a: To take small bets: present just the first slide on Friday, then one section at next month's board review, building proof step by step.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel reading that the idea of small bets is being tried?
qa.a: Vandana might feel glad and hopeful, and curious to hear how Friday goes.

grounding: Shows a young professional who wants a big role but avoids stretch tasks out of fear of failing, and plans small risks to build evidence.

subtype: Ambition mixed with fear of failure [Actor]
passage:
Ritu, I'll tell you what happened, but don't laugh. You know I've always said I want to lead the city desk someday. Big stories, my name on top. And for two years I pitched nothing. Nothing! Every Monday meeting I sat with three story ideas in my notes and said, 'I'll support whoever's on it.'
Last month I finally saw why. If I pitch and it flops, I'm just someone who wanted too much. If I never pitch, I can keep believing I'd be brilliant.
So I made a deal with myself: one small pitch a week. Tiny ones. A leaking water tank in a school. The editor took it and said, 'Good one, Himani.' Then a story about night-shift bus drivers. She took that too.
It's not the city desk. But now I have proof, not just hope. My hands still shake on Mondays, though.

qa.q: What was Himani's first small pitch?
qa.a: A leaking water tank in a school.

qa.q: Why did Himani avoid pitching for two years?
qa.a: Himani feared that a flop would mean being someone who wanted too much, while never pitching kept the belief in being brilliant safe.

qa.q: What choice helped Himani move past the fear, and why did it work?
qa.a: A deal of one small pitch a week; each accepted story built real proof, not just hope.

qa.q: How might the editor see Himani now compared with before?
qa.a: The editor may now see Himani as someone with ideas worth running, rather than a quiet supporter who never pitched.

grounding: Shows a young professional whose wish for a big role is held back by fear of failing, until small weekly risks start building evidence.
